title: VR, AR and Mixed Reality
summary: Stepping into digital worlds: the difference between virtual, augmented and mixed reality, how headsets trick your brain into believing, how AR apps understand the real world, how XR is used in training, health and education, how to use it safely and ethically, and how to design your own XR experience.
learn: The differences between VR, AR and mixed reality
How headsets use displays, lenses and tracking to create a sense of presence
How augmented reality apps understand and map the real world
How XR is used in training, healthcare, education and industry
The health, safety, privacy and ethical issues of XR
How to design a comfortable, user-centred XR experience
intro: Put on a headset and you're standing on Mars; hold up your phone and a dinosaur walks across the classroom; wear smart glasses and directions float in front of you. Virtual, augmented and mixed reality, together called extended reality (XR), are changing how we play, learn, train and work. In this topic you'll find out how XR tricks your senses, how phones understand the space around them, where XR is making a real difference, what risks it brings, and you'll design an XR experience of your own.

pages.title: The reality spectrum
pages.spec: Define VR, AR, mixed reality and XR and give examples of each
pages.summary: Virtual reality (VR) replaces the real world with a digital one. Augmented reality (AR) adds digital content on top of the real world. Mixed reality (MR) blends the two so digital objects interact with real ones. Together they're called extended reality (XR), and they sit on a spectrum from fully real to fully virtual.
pages.starter: What's the difference between watching a film, playing a video game and wearing a VR headset?
sc: I can define VR, AR and MR
I can place XR experiences on the reality spectrum
I can give examples of XR devices and apps

b: VR: replaces your surroundings with a digital world
AR: adds digital information on top of the real world
MR: digital objects that react to and interact with the real world
XR (extended reality): the umbrella term for all of them
Real world → AR → MR → VR → fully virtual
Phone AR: Snapchat filters, Pokémon GO, IKEA Place
Mixed reality headsets: Meta Quest 3, Apple Vision Pro
VR: games, virtual field trips, simulations
Phones and tablets: the most common AR devices
Standalone headsets: everything built in, no PC needed
Passthrough: cameras show you the real room inside a headset
Smart glasses: lightweight; cameras, audio and small displays

blocks.caption: VR, AR and MR
head: Type
What it does
Example
rows: Replaces the real world with a computer-generated one
Exploring the International Space Station in a headset

blocks.text: **[[extended reality|Extended reality]]** (XR) is the umbrella term for all three.

These technologies sit on a spectrum. At one end is the real world with nothing added; at the other is a completely virtual world. AR sits near the real end, VR at the virtual end, and MR in between. Modern headsets can move along the spectrum: with "passthrough" cameras they can show your real room with digital objects added, then fade it away to full VR.
**[[immersion|Immersion]]** describes how completely an experience surrounds your senses. VR is the most immersive because it blocks out the real world.

blocks.title: Types of XR device
items: Phones and tablets: the most common way people use AR (camera plus screen)
Standalone headsets (e.g. Meta Quest): all the computing is built in
High-end mixed reality headsets (e.g. Apple Vision Pro): very high-resolution displays and eye and hand tracking
Smart glasses: look like normal glasses, with cameras, speakers and sometimes small displays; increasingly include AI assistants
PC-powered headsets: connect to a powerful computer for detailed graphics

pages.title: Tricking the brain
pages.spec: Explain how XR headsets use displays, lenses, tracking and low latency to create presence, and why motion sickness happens
pages.summary: Headsets show a slightly different image to each eye so your brain sees depth (stereoscopic 3D). Lenses make the screens fill your view. Sensors and cameras track your head and hands with six degrees of freedom. High refresh rates and low latency keep the image in step with your movements; when they don't match, people can feel sick.
pages.starter: Hold a finger in front of your face and close one eye, then the other. What happens?
sc: I can explain how stereoscopic displays create depth
I can explain tracking and six degrees of freedom
I can explain presence, latency and motion sickness

b: Your eyes see slightly different views; your brain combines them to judge depth
Headsets show a different image to each eye: stereoscopic display
Lenses focus the screens and stretch them to fill your field of view
Higher resolution reduces the "screen door" effect
3DoF: tracks head turning only
6DoF: tracks turning AND moving: up/down, left/right, forward/back
Inside-out tracking: cameras on the headset map the room
Hand and eye tracking let you interact without controllers
Presence: the feeling of really being there
Needs high refresh rate (90 Hz or more) and low latency (under about 20 ms)
If what you see doesn't match what your inner ear feels, you may feel sick
Comfort settings: teleport movement, snap turning, vignettes

blocks.text: Your eyes are a few centimetres apart, so each sees a slightly different view. Your brain combines them to judge depth. A headset uses a **[[stereoscopic]]** display: it shows a slightly different image to each eye, so your brain sees a 3D world. Lenses focus the nearby screens and spread the image to fill your **[[field of view]]**, the area you can see without moving your eyes.

blocks.caption: Degrees of freedom
head: Type
Tracks
Example
rows: Rotation only: looking up/down, left/right, tilting your head
Rotation AND movement: stepping forward/back, left/right, crouching

blocks.text: Modern headsets use inside-out tracking: cameras and motion sensors on the headset watch the room and work out how you're moving, with no external sensors needed. Many also track your hands (so you can pinch and grab without controllers) and your eyes (so you can select things by looking).
**[[presence|Presence]]** is the feeling of really "being there" in a virtual world. It depends on smooth, responsive graphics:

items: **Refresh rate**: the screen should update at least 90 times a second (90 Hz).
**[[latency|Latency]]**: the delay between moving your head and the image changing should be under about 20 milliseconds.

blocks.title: Frames and time
steps: 90 frames are drawn every second.
Time per frame = 1,000 ms ÷ 90 ≈ 11 ms.
blocks.answer: The computer has only about 11 milliseconds to draw each image for both eyes, which is why XR needs powerful but efficient chips.

blocks.text: **[[motion sickness|Motion sickness]]** in XR happens when your eyes say you're moving but your inner ear (your balance sense) says you're standing still. Designers reduce it with teleport movement instead of smooth walking, "snap" turning, and vignettes that narrow your view while you move.

blocks.title: Depth and delay experiments
steps: Try the finger test: hold a pencil at arm's length and try to touch its tip with another pencil using one eye, then both eyes. Record your success rate.
Use a cardboard viewer or stereo image cards (if available) to see 3D.
Watch two video clips: one smooth and one with lag (your teacher will provide them). Describe how each feels.
Explain your results using stereoscopic, latency and presence.

q.q: Why was it harder to touch the pencil with one eye?
q.a: With one eye your brain loses the second viewpoint it uses to judge depth, so it's harder to tell how far away the pencil is. Stereoscopic headsets give each eye its own view to recreate this.

q.q: Why does lag make XR uncomfortable?
q.a: If the image updates late, what you see doesn't match how your head moved, breaking presence and causing a mismatch with your inner ear, which can make you feel sick.

o: It shows a different image to each eye to create depth

check.q: What does 6DoF tracking add compared with 3DoF?
o: Tracking movement, not just head rotation
The feeling of really being there

check.q: Why does XR motion sickness happen?
o: Your eyes and inner ear disagree about movement

practice.q: Explain how a headset creates a 3D image.
practice.a: Shows a slightly different image to each eye (1); the brain combines them to perceive depth (1).

practice.q: Describe three ways designers reduce motion sickness in VR.
practice.a: Any three: teleport movement (1); snap turning (1); vignettes (1); high refresh rate/low latency (1); stable horizon/seated experiences (1).

pages.title: AR in your pocket
pages.spec: Explain how AR apps detect and map the real world, and describe uses of AR
pages.summary: AR apps use the camera, motion sensors and computer vision to understand the real world. Marker-based AR recognises an image; markerless AR detects surfaces and tracks movement using SLAM; location-based AR uses GPS. This lets digital objects appear to sit in the real world, for games, shopping, navigation, translation and learning.
pages.starter: How does a phone know where your floor is, so a virtual sofa doesn't float in the air?
sc: I can describe marker-based, markerless and location-based AR
I can explain how SLAM lets a device map a space
I can describe useful applications of AR

b: Marker-based: recognises a picture or QR code and adds content to it
Markerless: detects floors, tables and walls to place objects anywhere
Location-based: uses GPS to show content at real places
Face tracking: maps facial features for filters
Camera images + motion sensors (accelerometer, gyroscope)
SLAM: Simultaneous Localisation And Mapping
Plane detection finds flat surfaces
Anchors keep virtual objects fixed in place as you move
Games: Pokémon GO, AR board games
Shopping: try on glasses, place furniture
Navigation: arrows in the street; car head-up displays
Translation: point at a sign and read it in your language

blocks.caption: Types of augmented reality
head: Type
How it works
Example
rows: Recognises a specific image or code and places content on it
Scan a textbook picture to see a 3D heart beating
Detects surfaces and tracks movement so objects can be placed anywhere
Placing a virtual sofa in your living room
Uses GPS and compass to show content at real-world locations
Maps facial features in real time

blocks.text: Markerless AR uses **[[SLAM]]** (Simultaneous Localisation And Mapping). As you move your phone, it:

items: Spots distinctive features in the camera image (corners, edges, patterns).
Uses motion sensors to measure how the phone is moving.
Builds a 3D map of the space while working out where the phone is within it.
Uses **[[plane detection]]** to find flat surfaces like floors, tables and walls.
Places virtual objects on an **[[anchor]]**, a fixed point in the map, so they stay in place as you walk around.

blocks.text: Some phones and headsets also have depth sensors (such as lidar) that measure distances directly, making mapping faster and more accurate.
AR struggles on plain white walls and shiny or dark surfaces, because there aren't enough distinctive features for the camera to track. Good lighting and textured surfaces help.

blocks.title: Useful AR
items: Education: 3D models of the solar system, the human body or historic buildings
Shopping: try on glasses or make-up; see furniture at full size in your room
Navigation: walking directions overlaid on the street; head-up displays in cars
Translation: point your camera at a sign or menu to translate it instantly
Maintenance: instructions overlaid on a machine to guide repairs
Accessibility: apps that describe surroundings for people with visual impairments

blocks.title: AR investigation
steps: Using a school tablet (or the demo videos), try an AR app that places objects (e.g. a measuring app or a 3D model viewer).
Test placing objects on different surfaces: carpet, desk, white wall, window. Record which work best.
Identify which type of AR the app uses.
Design an AR feature for your school (e.g. a tour for new Year 8 pupils).

q.q: Which surfaces worked best and worst, and why?
q.a: Best: textured desks and patterned carpet, which have lots of features to track. Worst: plain white walls and shiny windows, which have few features or reflect light.

q.q: Describe your AR feature for the school.
q.a: E.g. a location-based AR tour: new pupils point a tablet at classroom doors (markers) to see the teacher's name, a 3D model of what's taught there and arrows to the next room.

o: Flat surfaces like floors and tables

check.q: Why does AR struggle on plain white walls?
o: There are few distinctive features to track

practice.q: Describe how a markerless AR app places a virtual object on a table.
practice.a: Camera and motion sensors track features and movement (SLAM) (1); plane detection finds the flat table surface (1); object fixed to an anchor so it stays put (1).

practice.q: Describe two useful applications of AR other than games.
practice.a: Any two: education models (1); shopping try-on/furniture (1); navigation (1); translation (1); maintenance instructions (1); accessibility (1).

pages.title: XR at work and school
pages.spec: Describe how XR is used in training, healthcare, education and industry, and evaluate its benefits and limitations
pages.summary: XR lets people practise dangerous, expensive or rare situations safely, from surgery to firefighting. It's used for virtual field trips, therapy, design and remote help from experts. XR training can be effective and cheaper over time, but headsets cost money, can be uncomfortable, and can't fully replace real experience.
pages.starter: Which would you rather learn first in VR: flying a plane, performing surgery or defusing a bomb? Why?
sc: I can describe uses of XR in different industries
I can explain why XR is useful for training
I can evaluate the benefits and limitations of XR

b: Pilots have trained in flight simulators for decades
Surgeons rehearse operations in VR
Firefighters, police and soldiers practise emergencies
Mistakes in a simulation hurt no one
Virtual field trips: the Moon, the Titanic, inside a cell
Exposure therapy: facing fears like heights or spiders step by step
Pain distraction during treatment
Rehabilitation exercises turned into games
Architects walk clients through buildings before they're built
Engineers inspect digital twins of factories and products
Remote assistance: an expert sees what you see and draws instructions
Virtual meetings with 3D models

blocks.text: A **[[simulation]]** is a computer model of a real situation. XR simulations let people practise tasks that are dangerous, expensive or rare in real life.

blocks.caption: XR training
head: Who
What they practise
Why XR helps
rows: Too dangerous to practise for real
Practise before touching a real patient
Train without travelling or stopping production

blocks.text: A **[[virtual field trip]]** lets classes visit places they could never go: the surface of Mars, the inside of a volcano, a human cell or ancient Rome. In healthcare, **[[exposure therapy|VR exposure therapy]]** helps people overcome phobias (like fear of heights or flying) by facing them gradually and safely, and VR is used to distract patients from pain and to make rehabilitation exercises more engaging.

items: Architects let clients walk through buildings before they're built.
Car designers review full-size 3D models in VR rather than building expensive physical prototypes.
With **[[remote assistance]]**, a worker wears AR glasses or uses a tablet, and an expert far away sees what they see and draws instructions into their view.
Digital twins of factories let engineers spot problems and test changes virtually.

blocks.caption: Weighing up XR in education and training
head: Benefits
Limitations
rows: Headsets are expensive, especially for a whole class
Some people feel sick or uncomfortable
Experience places you couldn't otherwise visit
Can't fully replace real-world practice and touch
Needs space, charging and technical support
Can save travel, materials and money over time
Isolating if overused; less face-to-face interaction

pages.title: Safe and ethical XR
pages.spec: Describe the health, safety, privacy and ethical issues of XR and how to use it responsibly
pages.summary: XR can cause motion sickness, eye strain and accidents if you can't see your surroundings. Headsets collect very personal data, such as room scans, eye movements and body motion. Social VR can expose users to harassment. Age guidance, safety boundaries, privacy settings and good habits make XR safer.
pages.starter: What could go wrong if you wore a VR headset in a busy classroom?
sc: I can describe physical health and safety risks of XR
I can explain the privacy risks of XR data
I can describe how to stay safe in social VR

b: You can't see real obstacles: clear the space, set a boundary
Motion sickness, eye strain and headaches: take regular breaks
Most headsets are not designed for young children; check the age guidance
Keep the lenses out of direct sunlight (they can focus it and burn the screen)
Headsets scan your room with cameras
Eye tracking shows what you look at and for how long
Body movements can be unique enough to identify you
This data could reveal health, emotions and interests
Avatars meet and talk in shared virtual spaces
Harassment can feel very real because of presence
Use personal boundary settings, mute, block and report
Check age ratings and never share personal information

blocks.title: Using XR safely
items: Clear a safe play area and set up the **[[guardian boundary]]**, the virtual wall that warns you when you're near real obstacles
Take a break every 20-30 minutes, and stop if you feel sick, dizzy or have eye strain
Check the manufacturer's age guidance: many headsets are for ages 10 or 13 and over, with parental supervision for younger users
Make sure the headset fits and the lenses are adjusted for your eyes
Never leave headset lenses in direct sunlight

blocks.text: XR devices collect far more personal data than a phone or laptop. Cameras scan your home; microphones hear conversations; sensors track your head, hands and eyes. Eye tracking and body movement are **[[biometric data]]**, and researchers have shown that just a few minutes of movement data can identify someone among thousands of users. Eye movements might reveal interests, emotions, or even signs of health conditions.

blocks.caption: XR data and privacy risks
head: Data collected
What it could reveal
rows: The inside of your home, valuable items, other people
What you look at and find interesting; possibly health signs
Your identity, age, height, possibly disabilities

blocks.text: **[[social VR|Social VR]]** apps let people meet as avatars in shared virtual spaces. Because presence makes VR feel real, harassment, bullying or unwanted behaviour can feel as upsetting as it would in real life.

blocks.title: Staying safe in social VR
items: Check the **[[age rating]]** and only use apps suitable for your age
Use personal boundary or "safe zone" features that stop avatars getting too close
Mute, block and report anyone who makes you uncomfortable
Never share personal information such as your full name, school or location
Tell a trusted adult if something upsets you
Should companies use eye-tracking data to target adverts?
How should children's use of XR be protected?
If people spend long periods in virtual worlds, what happens to real-world relationships?
Who's responsible for behaviour in virtual spaces: users, platforms or governments? (The UK's Online Safety Act applies to many online platforms, including some VR spaces.)

Include a physical safety checklist, a "feeling unwell" plan and privacy settings to check.
Add a social VR code of conduct.
Design it as a one-page poster.

q.a: Treat others as you would face to face; respect personal space and use boundary settings; never share personal information; mute, block and report problems and tell a teacher.

practice.a: Any three: colliding with obstacles/falling (1); motion sickness (1); eye strain/headaches (1); unsuitable for young children (1); sunlight damage to lenses (1).

pages.title: Design an XR experience
pages.spec: Design a comfortable, accessible and purposeful XR experience using user-centred design and storyboarding
pages.summary: Good XR design starts with a clear purpose and real users. Designers storyboard the experience, choose how users move and interact, follow comfort guidelines and make it accessible. Prototypes can be made on paper or with easy XR building tools, then tested with users.
pages.starter: What's the best VR or AR experience you've tried or seen? What made it good?
sc: I can plan an XR experience for a real purpose and audience
I can choose interaction and movement methods that are comfortable and accessible
I can storyboard and prototype an XR experience

b: Does it need to be XR? What does XR add?
Who are the users? How old? Any accessibility needs?
What should users learn, feel or do?
How long will they spend in it?
Interaction: controllers, hand tracking, gaze, voice
Movement: teleport, snap turn, seated or standing
Keep text large and near the centre of view
Audio cues help users know where to look
Storyboard each scene: what the user sees, hears and does
Prototype with paper, or tools like CoSpaces Edu
Test with real users; watch where they get stuck
Improve and test again

blocks.text: Before designing an XR experience, ask: **does this need to be XR?** XR is best when it lets people do something they couldn't otherwise: see at real scale, step inside something, practise something risky or explore somewhere far away. Then think about the users: their age, experience, any accessibility needs, and how long they'll spend in it.
**[[interaction design|Interaction design]]** is about how users control and respond to an experience.

blocks.title: XR comfort and accessibility guidelines
items: Use teleport or snap turning; avoid sudden camera movements
Keep important text large, high-contrast and near the centre of view
Offer a seated mode so users who can't stand can take part
Use sound and subtitles together
Let users adjust height, speed and brightness
Keep sessions short and give clear ways to exit

blocks.text: Good **[[accessibility]]** means people with different abilities can enjoy the experience, for example by offering one-handed controls, seated modes and subtitles.

A **[[storyboard]]** is a series of sketches showing each scene: what users see, hear and do. A **[[prototype]]** is an early version for testing; it can be paper sketches arranged around the room, or a quick build in an XR creation tool such as CoSpaces Edu. **[[user testing|User testing]]** means watching real people try it, noting where they get confused or uncomfortable, and improving the design.

blocks.title: XR design sprint
steps: Choose a brief: an AR tour of Enniskillen Castle, a VR experience showing what's inside a computer, or an AR guide for new pupils.
Write a purpose statement and describe your users.
Storyboard at least four scenes, showing what the user sees, hears and does, plus how they move and interact.
Add comfort and accessibility features, then test your storyboard with another group and improve it.

q.q: Write your purpose statement and explain why XR suits it.
q.a: E.g. "A VR experience that shrinks Year 8 pupils to the size of an electron so they can travel through a computer's CPU, RAM and storage. XR suits this because pupils can see the inside of a computer at a scale that's impossible in real life."

q.q: Describe two comfort or accessibility features and one change you made after testing.
q.a: E.g. teleport between components instead of flying; subtitles and narration together. After testing: moved labels closer to the centre because testers missed them at the edge of their view.

check.q: What should be the first question when designing an XR experience?
o: Does this need to be XR, and what does XR add?
A series of sketches showing each scene
Tiny text at the edge of view
It shows where real users get stuck or uncomfortable

practice.q: Describe three guidelines for making a VR experience comfortable.
practice.a: Any three: teleport/snap turning (1); avoid sudden movements (1); large central text (1); seated mode (1); short sessions (1); high frame rate (1).

practice.q: Explain why designers prototype XR experiences on paper before building them.
practice.a: Quick and cheap to make changes (1); can test ideas with users before spending time/money on building (1).
